openers.measuring-an-economy: Before anyone can say whether an economy is doing well, someone has to decide what to count. This chapter gathers the measuring tools. Some describe things that exist at one moment, like a nation's machines or the skills and health of its workers, while others describe things that happen over time, like a year's output. Some boil the movement of many prices down to a single number. And some reach past the economy to the environment, which supplies materials and absorbs the waste that comes back.

nature-econ-531.title: Human capital: the skills people carry to work
nature-econ-531.text: Adam Smith counted 'the acquired and useful abilities' of a society's members as capital, alongside its machines and buildings. Economists now call this human capital: the knowledge, skills, know-how, health and education people bring to producing goods and services. Irving Fisher may have first used the term, and Pigou wrote that people can build up human capital just as they build up material capital. Just as land came to be seen as natural capital, the human inputs among the {{ref:nature-econ-086}} came to be seen as human capital. Unlike money capital, it tends to grow steadily over long periods, built on education and health. It also has an odd property for an asset. A firm cannot own it, so it leaves when employees leave. It strongly shapes what people earn, and spending on it pays high returns through childhood and young adulthood. Gary Becker's theory holds that education and training raise efficiency and growth, an argument often used to justify public subsidies for schooling and job training.

nature-econ-594.title: Stocks and flows: what you have versus what moves
nature-econ-594.text: Michał Kalecki once called economics 'the science of confusing stocks with flows'. The joke rests on a simple distinction. A stock is a quantity that exists at one point in time. A flow is a quantity measured per unit of time. Suppose a country has 20 machines on 1 January 2010 and 23 a year later. The machine count on each date is a stock. The change between them, 3 machines per year, is a flow, the country's net new equipment for 2010. A nation's whole capital stock works the same way: the flow of new machines and buildings adds to it, and the flow of wear and tear drains it. Capital itself is a stock that yields a periodic income, which is a flow. Because stocks and flows have different units, they cannot be added or compared directly. A nation's capital stock is measured in dollars, while its yearly output is measured in dollars per year. Their ratios still make sense. A country's debt divided by its yearly output gives a figure measured in years. Irving Fisher formalized the distinction in economics in 1896, and it runs through everything that follows in this chapter.

nature-econ-580.title: Productivity: getting more out of the same inputs
nature-econ-580.text: Simply piling on more workers and machines makes an economy bigger, but it does not raise income per unit of input. Productivity does. It measures how efficiently goods or services are produced, usually as output per unit of input over a period. The most common measure, {{ref:nature-econ-581}}, divides output by the number of workers. Measures that use one kind of input, such as worker hours, materials or energy per unit of output, are called partial productivities. Rising productivity can lift living standards, because higher wages let people buy more, enjoy leisure, and improve their housing and education. The gains can also go to owners as profits, consumers as lower prices, governments as taxes, and the environment when less resource or pollution goes into each unit. Pollution works in reverse. Counting lost labour and welfare, the World Bank put the global cost of air pollution at over $8 trillion per year.

nature-econ-590.title: Social capital: the value of trust and networks
nature-econ-590.text: In 1916 Lyda Hanifan, writing about local support for rural schools, used a phrase that would not catch on for decades. Social capital means the networks of relationships, built on trust, shared norms and give-and-take, that help people and groups reach their goals. The term became widely used only in the late 1990s. Pierre Bourdieu set it beside two other forms of capital, economic and cultural. Francis Fukuyama argues it forms through repeated dealings over time, is critical for development, and is hard for public policy to create. Knack and Keefer (1996) found that trust and civic cooperation strongly affect a country's growth. Communities rich in social capital also appear to enjoy better health. Critics, though, say the concept is imprecisely defined. Like natural capital, it has grown a separate literature of its own as a modern type of capital.

nature-econ-519.title: Depreciation: the value an asset loses as it ages
nature-econ-519.text: Every machine wears out, and accountants have a word for the value it loses along the way. Depreciation is the fall in an asset's value as it is used and wears out, and the spreading of its original cost over the years it stays useful. Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both accounting and tax purposes. The charge lowers reported net income, yet no cash leaves the business when it is recorded. The idea has close cousins. For resources such as oil the matching idea is {{ref:nature-acct-107}}, and for intangible assets it is amortization. When an asset's value falls unexpectedly, the loss is recorded instead as an impairment charge.

nature-econ-604.title: Financial capital: the money that buys the machines
nature-econ-604.text: A tailor's sewing machine is capital you can touch. The money that bought it is capital of a different kind. Financial capital is money, and other resources measured in money, that businesses use to buy what they need to produce goods or services. It comes from a firm's retained earnings, the profits it keeps, or from lenders and investors. Lenders charge a price for it: interest. Firms spend it on real capital, the physical goods that help produce other goods. Fixed capital buys lasting assets, while working capital pays for stock, running expenses and credit. Some ecological economists want natural capital added to the usual analysis of land, labour and financial capital. The link already shows in commodity markets, which respond to anything that affects natural capital, such as weather that damages food crops.

nature-econ-506.title: The consumer price index: pricing a basket of shopping
nature-econ-506.text: Often every month, statisticians collect prices from a sample of shops and service businesses. The results feed the consumer price index, or CPI, a statistical estimate of the price level of the goods and services households buy. It is a {{ref:nature-econ-832}} calculated as the weighted average price of a market basket. The annual percentage change in the CPI is a standard measure of inflation. Governments and employers use it to adjust wages, salaries and pensions for inflation, and to convert money amounts into real values. The items in the basket are updated from time to time to follow changing spending habits. When a product is replaced by one of different quality, its price may be adjusted so the CPI shows price change rather than quality change. A statistical technique, {{ref:nature-val-092}}, is used in building it. The CPI is not a perfect measure of inflation or the cost of living, but it is a useful tool for tracking both.

nature-econ-534.title: Index numbers: one figure that tracks many
nature-econ-534.text: If a commodity's price doubles between 1960 and 1970, its index with 1960 as the base reads 200. That is the whole trick of an index number. It compares a value with a base value, usually set at 100. A single number can then track how a group of related figures, such as prices or employment, changes over time. The consumer price index is one example. Others include cost-of-living indexes, stock market indices such as the S&P 500, and commodity indices. Some compare places rather than times, as {{ref:nature-econ-583}} does for currencies. Either way, index numbers turn complex data into figures that are easy to compare.

nature-econ-599.title: Total factor productivity: the growth nobody can explain
nature-econ-599.text: Robert Solow (1957) called it 'technical change', shorthand for any shift in the production function. Total factor productivity, or TFP, is the ratio of total output to total inputs: how much output a given bundle of inputs yields. Nobody measures it directly. Its growth is whatever part of output growth is left after counting growth in measured labour and capital, so it is calculated as a residual. For small changes, TFP growth is roughly output growth minus the growth of labour and capital inputs, usually weighted 0.7 for labour and 0.3 for capital. The leftover is large. Easterly and Levine estimated in 2001 that it accounts for 60 percent of growth in output per worker in an average country. Official statisticians prefer the name multifactor productivity, because inputs such as energy are left out, as are costs like the using up of minerals and pollution. Some economists consider TFP invalid, or at least in need of careful interpretation. Critics say it lacks meaningful units and may be a modelling artefact.

nature-econ-553.title: Source and sink: the environment's two jobs
nature-econ-553.text: The environment does two jobs for the economy. As a source, it supplies materials and services. As a sink, it absorbs and neutralizes waste and pollution. Natural inputs flow into production, and once consumed they leave the economy as pollution and waste. Both jobs can be overloaded. The source runs down as resources are used up or polluted. When waste exceeds the sink's assimilative capacity, long-term damage follows. Some persistent pollutants, such as nuclear waste, are absorbed very slowly or not at all. This view changes the economist's basic picture. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} replaces the simple {{ref:nature-econ-502}} with a diagram in which solar energy sustains the natural inputs and services used in production.

nature-econ-595.title: Carbon in the air as a stock and flow problem
nature-econ-595.text: The carbon dioxide in the air is a stock, measured in tons. Emissions raise it and sequestration, the capture and storage of carbon, lowers it, both measured in tons per day. Mathematically, a stock is the accumulation of inflows minus outflows over time. Seen this way, {{ref:nature-clim-149}} is a stock-and-flow problem: to shrink the stock of heat-trapping gases in the air, cut emissions and pull more carbon dioxide back out. Earth system science is full of such problems, from the cycles of carbon, nitrogen and water to Earth's energy budget. Stocks and flows are also the building blocks of the models in {{ref:nature-es-077}}, where Jay Forrester called them levels and rates.

nature-econ-532.title: Ranking countries by their human capital
nature-econ-532.text: Years in a classroom are not the same as learning. The World Bank's Human Capital Index, launched in October 2018, ranks countries by how much they put into young people's education and health care. It harmonized learning data across 164 countries, measuring knowledge actually gained rather than years of schooling alone. The World Economic Forum has published a Global Human Capital Index annually since 2012. The gaps between countries are vast. One measure of expected human capital put Finland highest, at 28.4 adjusted years between ages 20 and 64, and Niger lowest, at under 1.6.

nature-econ-582.title: The productivity paradox: new technology, slow gains
nature-econ-582.text: New technology should make workers more productive. Yet in the United States, overall productivity growth stayed slow from the 1970s to the early 1990s, and again from the 2000s to the 2020s. This puzzle is the productivity paradox. Several causes have been proposed, but there is no consensus on why growth slowed. The debate has also shifted. It now asks not just whether computers raise productivity but whether the potential for productivity growth is running out.

nature-econ-591.title: Bonding and bridging: two kinds of social ties
nature-econ-591.text: A criminal gang and a choir both build social capital, but not the same kind. Bonding social capital is the ties within groups of similar people, as in a gang. Bridging social capital is the ties between socially different groups, like those formed in choirs and bowling clubs. The harmful effects of social capital are more often linked to bonding than to bridging. Daniel Aldrich adds a third type, linking capital: the relationship between a person and a government official or elected leader. He applies these ideas to disaster recovery, studying Japan after the 2011 Fukushima meltdown.

nature-econ-593.title: Measuring social capital: how do you count trust?
nature-econ-593.text: How do you count trust? Researchers try trust surveys, network name generators that ask people to list their contacts, and counts of group membership. None settles the matter. There is no widely held consensus on how to measure social capital, and the dispute has become a debate in itself. Part of the difficulty is that social capital emerges as individuals take part in groups, rather than being held by any one person. Since 2016 the UN Sustainable Development Group's World Social Capital Monitor has used anonymous surveys of trust, solidarity and willingness to fund public goods.

nature-econ-592.title: When strong ties do harm
nature-econ-592.text: Strong group ties are not always good news. Negative social capital is the harmful side, where tight bonds produce bad outcomes for society. Research has linked civic associations to the rise of fascist movements. Pierre Bourdieu showed how social connections can reproduce inequality by giving insiders access to powerful positions. Without bridging ties to outsiders, bonding groups can become cut off from the rest of society. Scholars disagree on how much weight this deserves: Putnam sees social capital as positive, while a sizable literature finds it can do harm.

nature-econ-520.title: Three ways to spread an asset's cost over time
nature-econ-520.text: Take a machine that costs $70,000, will fetch $10,000 at the end of its life, and is expected to make 6,000 units. That end value is its salvage value. Units-of-production depreciation charges $10 for each unit made, so years of heavy use carry heavy charges. Straight-line depreciation, the simplest and most common method, divides cost minus salvage value evenly across the years of useful life. Declining-balance and sum-of-years-digits methods write off more in early years, assuming assets are most productive when new. Some methods follow the calendar; others follow use.

nature-econ-605.title: Leverage: running a business on borrowed money
nature-econ-605.text: Borrowing can magnify a business's profits, and its dangers. Leverage is the ratio between a firm's borrowed capital, its debt, and its own capital, its equity. Own capital comes from the owners, for example from money they have put aside or inherited. Borrowed capital comes through debt and usually must be repaid with interest. High leverage can bring higher profit, but it also raises the risk of insolvency, of being unable to pay what is owed.

nature-econ-584.title: The law of one price
nature-econ-584.text: Without transport costs or trade barriers, a good should sell for the same price everywhere. That is the law of one price. Real markets bend it. Transport costs and trade restrictions weaken it by making goods expensive to move between countries. Firms that sell the same product at different prices in different markets break it too. The principle still earns its keep: it is the basis of {{ref:nature-econ-583}}.

nature-econ-535.title: Why no price index is ever quite right
nature-econ-535.text: When prices rise, shoppers switch to cheaper goods. A fixed basket cannot see that switch, so the consumer price index misstates living costs. This substitution bias is one face of the index number problem. Statistical indices cannot perfectly measure economic change, because they rest on fixed assumptions such as a set basket of goods. The {{ref:nature-econ-526}} has its own version of the trouble, skewing real output by not fully adjusting for new products. There is no perfect fix. Statisticians update baskets and weights periodically, but long-term comparisons stay inexact.

nature-econ-601.title: Is productivity growth really about energy?
nature-econ-601.text: Over history, total factor productivity has risen and fallen in step with two things: energy use, and how efficiently energy is converted into useful work. Reiner Kümmel concluded that the unexplained leftover in growth, the residual that total factor productivity measures, can be explained very well by an economy's energy input. On this view, technical progress is the ability to absorb primary energy and turn it efficiently into useful energy for production. Much of what looks like ingenuity in the statistics may track the energy behind it.

nature-econ-579.title: Chained price indexes: updating the base every year
nature-econ-579.text: A price index anchored to one distant year slowly loses its grip. Unchained indices compare every period with a single fixed base, so their bias grows over time as the quantities people buy drift away from that base. A chained price index avoids this by updating its base every period and multiplying the period-to-period changes together. Each link compares only neighboring periods, and the chain carries the comparison across the years.

nature-econ-578.title: Elementary indices: the building blocks inside the CPI
nature-econ-578.text: Inside every large price index sit many small ones. Elementary price indices are unweighted indices that compare the prices of single items between periods, and they serve as building blocks for larger indices such as the CPI. The formula matters. The Carli index averages price ratios, and it is biased upward: a doubling and a halving average out to 1.25, not 1. The Jevons index, from 1863, takes the unweighted geometric mean of price relatives instead, the ratios of new prices to old.

nature-econ-575.title: The Laspeyres index: yesterday's basket at today's prices
nature-econ-575.text: In 1871 Étienne Laspeyres asked a simple question: what would the basket people bought in the base period cost at today's prices? His index measures exactly that. It is the easiest index to compute, because it needs only new price data, not new quantities. The simplicity has a price. By ignoring consumers who switch to cheaper goods when prices rise, it often overstates inflation.

nature-econ-576.title: The Paasche index: today's basket instead
nature-econ-576.text: Hermann Paasche flipped the approach in 1874. His index uses current-period quantities, the basket people buy now, rather than the basket of the base period. That makes it harder to compute than the Laspeyres index, since statisticians need fresh quantity data as well as prices. It also leans the other way. By assuming consumers adjust their purchases instantly to new prices, it understates inflation.

nature-econ-577.title: The Fisher index: splitting the difference
nature-econ-577.text: If one index runs high and another runs low, why not meet in the middle? The Fisher index is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices. It balances the Laspeyres tendency to overstate inflation against the Paasche tendency to understate it. It belongs to a class called superlative indices, introduced by W. Erwin Diewert in 1976 and preferred for measuring inflation and national output in {{ref:nature-econ-483}}.
